dialogs.title: Dialogue — Padinané Rini
dialogs.intro: Saturday night on the porch. Dian wonders how Rini always manages to get up early. A ngoko conversation full of daily routines and frequency words.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Rin, kowé kok isa tangi ésuk terus?
lines.id: Rin, how come you can always get up so early?
lines.literal: Rin, you how-come can wake-up morning always?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Wis kulina. Saben dina aku tangi jam lima.
lines.id: I'm used to it. I get up at 5:00 every day.
lines.literal: already used. every day I wake-up hour five.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Adus, salat, banjur nyapu. Sawisé kuwi lagi sarapan.
lines.id: Shower, pray, then sweep. Only after that do I have breakfast.
lines.literal: bathe, pray, then sweep. after that only breakfast.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: What time do you leave for class?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Setengah pitu. Kuliahé wiwit jam pitu.
lines.literal: half seven. lecture-the start hour seven.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: And when do you get home?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Biasané soré. Nanging Selasa karo Kemis aku kerja part-time.
lines.id: Usually in the afternoon. But on Tuesdays and Thursdays I work part-time.
lines.literal: usually afternoon. but Tuesday and Thursday I work part-time.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Ngajar les basa Inggris. Sithik-sithik, kanggo tambah dhuwit saku.
lines.id: Teaching English lessons. Just a little, for some extra pocket money.
lines.literal: teach lesson language English. little-little, for add money pocket.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Kerep. Nanging aku arang lara, mula ya wis.
lines.id: Often. But I'm rarely ill, so that's that.
lines.literal: often. but I rarely sick, so yes already.

notes: **Kok** here is different from the emphatic *kok* you met in unit 5. At the start of a sentence, *kok* means "how come, why" with a tone of surprise: *kok isa?* (how come you can?).
**Isa** is another form of *bisa* (can), and both are equally correct. In Yogyakarta *isa* is heard a little more often; in East Java, *iso*.
**Kulina** means "used to, accustomed"; the krama is also *kulina*. From the same root comes *kulinakaké* (to get used to). It is very handy for explaining habits: *aku wis kulina* (I'm used to it).

**Sawisé** means "after", from *sawis* + *-é*. The krama is *sasampunipun*. Its partner is *sadurungé* (before), krama *saderengipun*. Both stand at the start of the clause, just like English "after" and "before".
**Mula** means "so, therefore"; the krama is *milanipun*. It links cause and effect: *aku kesel, mula ora melu* (I'm tired, so I'm not coming).
**Dhuwit saku** — pocket money. Noun + noun with nothing in between, but in Javanese order: the main word comes first (*dhuwit*, money).

**Ya wis** at the end of a sentence means "oh well, that's that" — accepting a situation you can't change. It is one of the most Javanese expressions there is, and it carries the whole attitude often called *nrima* (acceptance).

grammars.title: Putting activities in order
body: To tell things in sequence, Javanese uses linking words placed just as in English. All you need is the vocabulary.
after: **Lan and karo both mean "and"**, but *karo* also means "with": *aku karo Rini* (Rini and I / I with Rini). If you clearly want "and" to join two sentences, use *lan*.
**Terus** is borrowed from Indonesian and is used for "then" just as often as *banjur*. Both are correct; *banjur* is a little neater.
These linking words are the whole storytelling toolkit you need at A1. Unit 20 uses them all at once.

blocks.text: **Dolan** has no exact English equivalent: it means to play, to visit, to wander about, and to drop in at a friend's house for no particular reason — all at once. *Ayo dolan* is an invitation you will hear very often, and it very rarely has a detailed plan behind it.

blocks.title: Bakul, tukang, and words that aren't insults
items: **Bakul** means a small trader — a market seller, a street vendor, a *warung* owner. In Javanese the word is **completely neutral**, even though in Indonesian slang the borrowed word can sound a little dismissive.

**Tukang** is also neutral, even slightly respectful: it means someone skilled at a trade. *Tukang kayu* (carpenter), *tukang batu* (bricklayer), *tukang cukur* (barber), *tukang becak* (pedicab driver) — all normal, respectful labels.
To be more polite when naming someone's job, put a form of address in front: *Pak tukang*, *Bu bakul*, *Mas sopir*.
